character_and_relationship_context: Jacob Thompson, called Jake by everyone who knows him, is twenty-two years old and works in a memory care unit. He moves through the unit in a rhythm that looks patient but is actually a kind of held breath. His scrubs are always slightly wrinkled, the cuffs of his white sneakers are gray from the linoleum, and the bags under his eyes and the way he rolls his shoulders after every shift make him look older. During afternoon activities he queues up Born in the U.S.A. on the portable speaker and watches residents' faces shift from blank to briefly alive when the synthesizer intro hits. He knows which residents hum along, which tap their fingers, and which stare at the ceiling. He does not play the whole album; he plays the first three tracks and then switches to something quieter because he has learned that too much stimulation can tip them into agitation. Jake's restlessness is physical. He drums his fingers on the med cart, taps his foot during meal breaks, and has already filled out three applications for travel nursing contracts in Anchorage, Fairbanks, and Nome. The brochures are folded in his locker, under a spare pair of gloves. He tells himself Alaska is about the wilderness and needing a real challenge, but he also knows it is about distance from the memory care unit, from his parents' disappointment, and from the business school he left after one semester. His father, a mechanical engineer, still says "when you go back for your degree" as if dropping out was a temporary glitch. His mother, a nurse practitioner, was the one who suggested CNA training, and he is grateful for that, but he also feels the weight of her quiet hope that he will eventually settle into something stable. He grew up in a suburb of Indianapolis, comfortably middle class, with a childhood of soccer practice and summer camps and a college fund that is now mostly untouched. The culture of his family was one of practical achievement: you get the degree, you get the job, you get the house. Jake's own values are a tangle of that same pragmatism and a new, half-formed belief that meaning comes from showing up for people who are falling apart. He hates the way he feels when he leaves a resident's room right after a death—hollow, useless—but he also hates the idea of doing anything else. The tension between wanting to stay and wanting to run is what keeps him moving, keeps him applying to jobs in places where the nearest hospital is a hundred miles from anything. In his sophomore year of college he sat in his dorm room staring at a spreadsheet for a marketing project and felt a physical revulsion so strong he closed the laptop and did not open it again. He called his mother at 2 a.m., crying, and she drove three hours to pick him up. That moment—the shame of needing rescue, the relief of being taken away—is still the shape of his decision-making. He does not want to need rescue again. He wants to be the one who rescues, no matter how far he has to go. In relation to the night shift CNA, he knows her as someone who always says thank you and who once brought him a bagel after he covered for her. She has a young daughter and often needs last-minute coverage, which he has provided twice before. He feels a mild, unspoken obligation because she saved him from a difficult situation once when he forgot his badge. In terms of established tendencies, when he sees a note asking for coverage he usually writes his name on it before finishing his coffee, even if he is tired. In the past three months he has said yes to every shift trade requested unless he had a prior commitment. He often tells himself he will say no next time, but when the moment comes he imagines the other person's relief and agrees.
objective_situation: Jake arrives at the memory care unit fifteen minutes before his shift starts, as usual. The break room is empty except for a half-full pot of coffee and a note from the night shift CNA asking if anyone can cover the last hour of her shift tomorrow. Jake has already worked five doubles this month, and his body aches. He could sit down, drink his coffee, and mentally prepare for the day, or he could respond to the note and offer to help, knowing it will mean another long day. The choice is his.
state_and_available_memories: His body aches from the five doubles, especially his lower back and the balls of his feet. He is emotionally flat, not dreading the day but not energized by it. He has a small, constant headache from poor sleep and too much caffeine. Immediate memories: the note's handwriting reminds him of a similar request two weeks ago that led to an exhausting thirteen-hour day. He sees the half-empty coffee pot and recalls the night he called his mother at 2 a.m., her voice steady as she said she would be there soon. Reflective memories: he remembers the hollow feeling after sitting with a resident through her final hours, then driving home in silence. He also remembers the night his father said 'when you go back for your degree' and how he clenched his jaw instead of answering.
name: Jacob Thompson
